title: Notes of Ministry - 48 - November 1976

paragraphs.text: Manifestation as it was considered in the previous meeting is from the divine side. The Lord manifesting His glory is obviously from His side. The works of God manifested in a man is also from the side of divine operations, so that there is the manifestation of something here. I desire to say something now about our side, because manifestation is one thing, but it is another thing to have eyes to see it. Our side is having eyes to see, and thus the ability to apprehend divine movements. The Lord might manifest His glory and there may be some persons who would see it and appreciate it, and there may be some who would not see it. The feast-master in John 2 saw the results, but did not know the secret. The servants knew. The mother of Jesus had eyes to see—she knew what was going on. The feast-master did not have eyes to see; he gives the credit to the bridegroom. How important it is therefore that we should have eyes to see, that our sight should be operative, and that we are no longer blind.

We are all blind by nature. None of us would have any apprehension or appreciation of divine manifestation naturally. It needs a divine work that we might have our eyes opened to see. The Lord says here in John 9 to the Pharisees, “Ye say, We see”. One of the greatest difficulties that we as believers have to face is that we think we see.

We say, ‘We see’, therefore we remain blind. We just need to take account of our own histories to prove how often we have missed the Lord’s manifestation because we have said, ‘We see’. The Pharisees in this chapter had their own ideas, their own set-up, their own religion, everything according to their own mind. They said, ‘We see’. If we are to have our eyes opened, dear brethren, to any of the Lord’s operations at the present time we have to come to it that we do not see. If we say, ‘We see’, be sure we remain blind. There are plenty around us who say they see. I do not desire to be personal but there are many persons who say, ‘We see’. If we have come at all into the light it is because we have had to admit that we do not see. This man in John 9 did not say, ‘I see’; he became the subject of the Lord’s operations so that he did see. One of the greatest obstacles to our seeing is that we are content with our own ideas. We say, ‘We see’.

Now we come to this incident in Mark’s gospel of a man who was blind. It says the Lord “comes to Bethsaida; and they bring him a blind man, and beseech him that he might touch him”. This man did not say, ‘I see’. He did not claim anything; he was willing to be the subject of the Lord’s own gracious operations. There was no rebellion with him; he did not impose his thoughts in any way; he just became the subject of the Lord’s movements and activities towards him. It says they “beseech him that he might touch him. And taking hold of the hand of the blind man ... ”. Think of that! If we want to see divine operations we have completely to submit ourselves under the Lord’s hand. He took hold of him by the hand. We read in Hebrews 2: 16, “He does not indeed take hold of angels by the hand, but he takes hold of the seed of Abraham”. Oh how good to be taken hold of by

the hand by the Lord Himself! How different from saying, ‘We see’. We do not help by argument persons who say they see, no matter how clear the arguments are, no matter how confirmed is the one who argues. What is needed is to submit oneself to the Lord Himself. “Taking hold of the hand of the blind man” was the beginning of the Lord’s operations with him. I wonder if we have all submitted to being taken hold of by the hand, young people here included. He will take you on in this way if you are subject, if you are willing. He will take you by the hand. You may have life before you, and it may seem uncertain, as it must be in a world like this. Older ones who may be in failing health, and may be nearing the end of their journey here, the Lord would take by the hand. Oh what a Priest He is! He is always available, ever living to intercede for us, ever thinking of us, ever ready to consider for us in every detail. It says, “Taking hold of the hand of the blind man”. That is the first step. Would you like to see the Lord when He manifests Himself, when He manifests His glory? Would you like to be one who manifests the works of God down here? This is the only way to it. This man was submissive to have his hand taken hold of by the Lord Jesus.

If the Lord takes hold of your hand, where will He lead you? He led this man out of the village, out of the influence of the village. There is city life and there is village life. In a city you could live near to someone for twenty years and not even know his name, but in a village everybody knows everybody. It is a closely knit social community. The Lord took him by the hand and led him forth out of the village, out of every other influence to be alone with Himself. This blind man was alone with the Lord. Oh how important that is! There may be persons around us who may be wondering where the

Lord is. They will not be helped by argument, neither will they be helped by going around to this place and that place. The way that any of us will get help is to allow the Lord to take us by the hand and bring us out of every wrong influence to be alone in His own presence. I have heard of young persons saying, ‘How do I know which company is right?’. I would like to say to such that if you are really interested to know what is right the Lord will show you. The Lord will show you if you are prepared to let Him take hold of you by the hand and be alone with Him. Nothing substitutes for being alone with the Lord. I am not minimising the importance of meetings and ministry, because these will all help as we know what it is to be alone with the Lord, away from every other influence.

Then it says, “having spit upon his eyes”. What can anyone say about that? Something is imparted from the Lord Himself. Something is imparted from Jesus as a real Man, yet in His Person He is God. His manhood is real. The spittle of Jesus; how holy the matter is! Something was in this world that was never here before, when Jesus became a Man. Something existed for the pleasure of God that never existed before. How wonderful is the incarnation! The greatest thing that ever happened in this universe is that one of the holy Trinity became flesh and became available to men as a Man, available to men and women and young people. Think of the Lord’s interest to spit upon his eyes. Something was imparted from Himself as this man was alone with Him. This happened literally to this man; something corresponding to this happens when we are alone with Him, out of the range of every other influence. He spat upon his eyes, and laid His hands upon him. The Lord committed Himself to this blind man. “He laid his hands upon him, and asked him if he beheld anything”. The man might

have said, ‘I see’. He did not say ‘I see’. What he said was, “I behold men, for I see them, as trees, walking”. This man was honest. He said exactly what he saw. His vision was imperfect. He might have said, ‘I have all I want now, I can see’, but he said, “I behold men, for I see them, as trees, walking”.

Many of us have been like this man. Just let us go over our histories not many years ago. How true it is that we saw men as trees walking! We had distorted vision, and it may be that we yet have distorted vision, for we are not all seeing eye to eye in everything. I am being very practical, but it is the truth, therefore there must be some distorted vision somewhere. It is not a question of everybody coming round to my view of things, or coming round to any man’s view of things. The secret is in allowing the Lord to take hold of us by the hand and lead us out of every other influence. In a village there is a good deal of prejudice, a good deal of personal preference. We need to get clear of every prejudice, every preference, and every such influence, and be alone with the Lord. This man had vision basically, but it was distorted, and we all tend to have this kind of vision, but it says, “Then he laid his hands again upon his eyes”. This is often spoken of as the second touch, but it does not say that the Lord laid His hands upon his eyes a second time. It says that He laid His hands again upon his eyes, not the second time, but again. My impression is that we need the Lord to lay His hands upon our eyes over and over again because we become so easily distorted because of influences.
I think I am justified in saying this because if we follow the history of Peter after this incident we see that he needed not only a second touch

but touch after touch. What follows this incident is the Lord saying, “Who do men say that I am?”, and Peter shows clear vision by saying “Thou art the Christ”. He can see clearly, but then just immediately afterwards the Lord said, “The Son of man must suffer many things”, and “Peter, taking him to him, began to rebuke him”. Think of that! Peter really said, ‘I see’, but Peter had distorted vision, and needed the Lord’s hands again to be laid upon his eyes. Then in the next chapter Peter, James and John are taken up to the mountain top, the place of great privilege, and Peter said, “Let us make three tabernacles, for thee one, and for Moses one, and for Elias one”. He sees men as trees walking, and he needs again the Lord’s hands to be laid upon his eyes. What we need, dear brethren, is the current laying on of the Lord’s hands on our eyes in every situation that may arise. It is not a once for all matter, nor is it only a second time matter—it is a thing we need again and again.

The apostle Peter in the early chapters of the Acts was mightily used of the Lord, but when we come to Acts 10, where God has in mind that the gospel should be preached to Cornelius the gentile, Peter has to get a special revelation. He has to see a certain vessel as a great sheet coming down out of heaven, and there was a voice saying, “Rise, Peter, slay and eat”. Peter said, “In no wise, Lord”. He thought he saw. He would say, ‘I see’. His vision was so distorted that he required this to happen three times. I am sure that over and over again in every current situation we need the Lord’s laying of His hands on our eyes, and that involves the process of being taken hold of by the hand and being led out of the village. We so tend to come under prejudice and personal preference or selfish interest that we need continually the Lord to lay His hands on our eyes. “Then he laid his

hands again upon his eyes, and he saw distinctly, and was restored and saw all things clearly”. Oh what a fine result that was! I wonder if we are all like that. I question myself if I am like that. There is no reason why any of us should not see distinctly and be restored and see all things clearly. He had seen distinctly before, apparently, but something had come in that needed the Lord to undertake all this service to him, and then he was restored and saw all things clearly. Now he would be able to see the Lord manifesting His glory; he would be one who would manifest the works of God; he would be one who would be available for the Lord to manifest Himself to. I trust this appeals to every one here. I trust it proves to be attractive, so that we desire to be like this man and finish with saying, ‘I see’; finish with laying down our own ideas and having our own thoughts and expecting everybody else to conform to them, and submit ourselves under the Lord’s hands so that we may all see things clearly.

Now it says, “He sent him to his house, saying, Neither enter into the village, nor tell it to anyone in the village”. It is interesting how the Lord in Mark 7 and 8 charges persons. It is a great matter to come under the Lord’s charge. In the previous chapter we have the deaf man who could not speak right. The Lord, having spit, groaned and said, “Ephphatha, that is, Be opened”. The Lord felt the process with this man. Then it says, “He charged them that they should speak to no one of it”. They are put under charge. It is a great matter, dear brethren, to accept charge. He charged them to speak to no one of it, but it says “so much the more he charged them, so much the more abundantly they proclaimed it”. We might think they did a good service. It says, “They were astonished above measure, saying, He does all things well; he makes

both the deaf to hear, and the speechless to speak”. We might have thought. What a fine service! Was it? “He charged them that they should speak to no one of it”. It was contrary to what He had charged them. We might think that they could not go wrong saying, “He does all things well”, but they were not obedient to the charge. It is a great matter to accept charge, to know what our charge is and to keep it. The Lord knows better than we do. We need to have our eyes opened, like this man in Mark 8, to know what the charge is, and to be obedient. “He sent him to his house, saying, Neither enter into the village, nor tell it to anyone in the village”. The charge was definite and direct and we trust he accepted it.

Now in verse 29 of our chapter when Peter says, “Thou art the Christ”, “He charged them straitly, in order that they should tell no man about him”. We are in the area here where the Lord is charging them, and if we are to be here for God’s will, and for the glory and pleasure of our Lord Jesus Christ, we need to come under charge, know what our charge is, and fulfil it. We are not to be left here to our own devices. We are not here to do what we think best. We had in the reading, “He that has my commandments and keeps them, he it is that loves me”. “If any one love me, he will keep my word”, John 14: 21, 23. It is a question of having the commandment and keeping it, and keeping His word.
Come under charge, accept responsibility, and be committed for the glory and pleasure of our Lord Jesus Christ. May it be so on the part of everyone, for His name’s sake.

1 Kings 18: 30, 37–39, 41–45 (first clause); Malachi 3: 10; 1 Corinthians 2: 9–I want to draw attention first to the fulness of blessing which is in God’s heart, and then to the way that people like ourselves may come into it. It is one glorious fact that the heart of God is full of the most unbounded and abiding blessing for His creature, but there is a way into it. I would like to say at the very outset that there has been established for God, by our Lord Jesus Christ Himself, an abiding basis upon which God is completely free to bless. It is referred to in this chapter of 1 Kings. Elijah, the man of God, the prophet, he had an appreciation of what it was. He realised, too, that the basis had been laid—not for a few, but for the whole of God’s people, and he demonstrated by what he did that this truth was not only in his mind but in his heart for “he repaired the altar of Jehovah which was broken down. And Elijah took twelve stones”—twelve stones, one for each tribe, so that the altar represented all the people of God. On that altar he put a sacrifice, and then he did what would seem to be extraordinary. He not only laid the wood there, but he commanded that three times water should be poured both on the sacrifice and on the wood, and in the trench that he dug round the altar. Then he called upon God, in whom he had complete confidence, to demonstrate that He Himself was identified with what he had done—that is, that which spoke of the sacrifice and death of Christ in
relation to all the people. And demonstrate it He did!

The divine answer was that the fire came down. It “fell, and consumed the burnt-offering, and the wood, and the stones, and the dust, and licked up the water that was in the trench”. The burnt-offering is wholly for God. It is what Christ has effected for God. It is not the sin-offering. The sin-offering is burnt at the place of the burnt-offering, but this is the burnt-offering. This is the aspect of the death of Christ as meeting all that the heart of God requires, that that heart might be liberated in the fulness of the blessing that is in it. Beloved brethren, let us for a moment focus our minds and our affections on this aspect of the death of Christ and let us, as laying hold of it, understand that God Himself is free to pour out into your soul and mine the fulness of the knowledge of Himself, which is blessing, and blessing unbounded.

Then the people acknowledge that God had indeed intervened, and what happened was this— that those people, who were indeed the people of God, were brought back to the basic foundation upon which God could, and ever did, move towards them. I would suggest that it is a good thing ever to keep this aspect of the death of Jesus in mind. We, because of what we are, necessarily think of the sin-offering—and how thankful we are for the sin-offering! Think of the blood of the sin-offering being taken right into God in the tent of meeting! How thankful we are that Jesus died for our sins! I said to a boy (not one who knew the Lord Jesus), ‘If somebody was prepared to take the punishment for something that you knew you had done that was wrong, what would you think of the person who did it?’. Do you know what he said? ‘I would like him very much’.

Ah! is that not the secret of love for Christ—what He has done for you? You love Him, do you, because of what He has done for you? You know that you deserved to be punished, but He bore the punishment instead. Oh how we love Him for that! But then we begin to love Him because of who He is and what He is. It is not only what He has done, but it is the One who has done it!

It was at the time of the oblation that all this happened in our scripture. It was at the time when the manhood of Jesus was cherished, typically, in the heart of this offerer, at that time, that attention was called to this foundation which God has, that He might be free to bless. Well now, that is His side. But there are certain necessary elements that come in on our side. Do you know what one is? Prayer. Do you know what another one is? It is in Malachi— unreserved committal as to what is due to God. And a third thing is—taking advantage of the wonderful grace that has given us the Holy Spirit that we might understand, and lay hold of, “the things which have been freely given to us of God”. Prayer, committal, and the Holy Spirit—Do you think that is sufficient resource? What I would say to every heart here, is, ‘Let us take it on’. Think of that man Elijah. He “put his face between his knees”. What does it mean? I believe it means complete self-abnegation—the setting aside of self altogether in utter dependence upon God! But he prayed believing! “He prayed with prayer”, James 5: 17. And when he sent his servant to see if there was any answer to his prayer, he expected that there would be an answer—and there was none!
Have you ever prayed and it seems as if God does not answer your prayer? Have you ever done that? I have! What do you do? Give up? Do

not give up! Keep praying! Keep on, and let us keep in mind all the time, that the basis for God to bring to pass blessing is already laid. No one will ever interfere with it. No one can ever take away from it, and it is not necessary that anything should be added to it, because it is perfect and complete in the Man who is in the presence of God at this very moment. So keep praying, seven times! Perhaps you say, ‘That prophet must have been tested’. I have no doubt he was, but he never lost faith. Maybe there is somebody here with a problem. I do not know; God knows. Maybe somebody is carrying a burden. Maybe there is a need that does not seem to be met. I say, ‘Keep on praying’, because there is blessing in the heart of God. And pray in faith! That servant came back. “And it came to pass at the seventh time that he said, Behold there is a cloud, small as a man’s hand, arising out of the sea”.

It was just as if God was showing His hand in relation to the thing that the prophet desired. And do you know, beloved brethren, I believe that God is showing His hand at the present time, and He is showing His hand in blessing. This rain represents blessing, because Hebrews 6: 7 says, “Ground which drinks the rain which comes often upon it, and produces useful herbs … partakes of blessing from God”. There is an abundance of blessing, and there are indications at the present time that this is happening. Do you believe that? I am persuaded that it is so. Then I say, let us pray, as we see the indications that God is going to bless. There is only one cloud to start with but presently, it says, “the heavens became black with clouds”. I wonder if any of us think that God is withholding His hand in blessing? That does not mark the blessed God! He does not, I was going to say, dole out things in small quantities. That is not

the God I know. He is a God who is rich in mercy, marked by abundance of grace, and He is prepared to intervene for His own sake, and to pour out a blessing upon His creature so that there is response from that creature for Himself.

So it says, “And it came to pass in the mean while, that the heavens became black with clouds and wind, and there was a great pour of rain. And Ahab got on the chariot, and went to Jizreel”. Elijah had said, “There is a sound of abundance of rain”, abundance of blessing, and presently it came to pass. I say to my soul, and I say to yours, ‘Let us keep constantly in prayer’. Do you know, prayer moves the hand of God. Mr. Taylor said that prayer brings God in, and fasting keeps man out, and that it well worth thinking about, and putting into practice too.

In Malachi, which relates to a day when, outwardly, things were very dark publicly. God says to His people, through the prophet, “Bring the whole tithe into the treasure-house, that there may be food in my house, and prove me now herewith, saith Jehovah of hosts, if I open not to you the windows of the heavens, and pour you out a blessing, till there be no place for it”, or ‘to superabundance’ (see N.T. footnote). Bring the whole tithe and then prove Me! It is God saying this. God’s things are to be proved; and when you prove a thing, you know, nobody could ever tell you that it is not true. It is when you have never proved a thing and it is in your head and not in your heart, that you get shaky. I am speaking very simply; I would like the young people especially to be helped in the practical side of the truth, but I want to stimulate the older ones too. Because, you know, it is continuance that tests us. Jehovah says, “Bring the whole tithe into the
treasure-house”. We sing—
‘Should we not then devoted be,
In full committal, Lord, to Thee’.

It often comes to this, that some consideration, which I think may be due to me, takes away something that is due to God. Is that not right? And if I take that line, you may be sure that I shall become impoverished. But if I am prepared, maybe at some self-sacrifice, maybe at some inconvenience to myself, to bring the whole tithe to the treasure-house, so that there is food in God’s house. God says, ‘You prove Me, and see what I will do for you. I will pour you out a blessing to superabundance’. What a God He is! Who has proved Him? Could I ask another question? Who has not? I say, If you have not, dear soul, from today give Him what is due to Him. You say, ‘What is that?’. It is you! Give Him yourself! Take a step in Romans 12: 1. Present your body “a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your intelligent service”. See what He will do for you! “Prove me now ... if I open not to you the windows of the heavens, and pour you out a blessing, till there be no place for it”. The character of the blessing is heavenly. It stands related to an appreciation of, and participation in, what is of Christ and the assembly, and there is nothing more blessed than to have an appreciation of what the assembly is to Christ, and to participate in the response to Himself.

When we come to Corinthians there is a divine Person available in the blessed Spirit Himself. It says first, “Things which eye has not seen, and ear not heard, and which have not come into man’s heart, which God has prepared for them that love him”. In this section the man referred to is the natural man; not exactly the fleshly man or the wicked man or the evil man, but the natural man.

The footnote says, ‘the man animated merely by his created soul, without the teaching and power of the Holy Spirit’. These things have not come into that man’s mind, his ear has not heard about them, and they have not come into his heart, but God has prepared them “for them that love him”. How are they to become available? By the service in power of the blessed Spirit! There are three books of Mr. J. Taylor’s ministry, a little larger in size than the usual ones—‘The Service of God’, ‘The Assembly’, and ‘The Holy Spirit’. I commend these three books to you. In the last there is a chapter entitled, ‘The Holy Spirit in Romans’, and in it Mr. Taylor says that the best Friend we have on earth is the Holy Spirit of God. I want to encourage your heart, and stimulate my own, to take full advantage of what, to use his words, this best Friend would do for us. You see, the things we are speaking about are spiritual realities, and you need the Holy Spirit to understand them. I would encourage simple, confiding intercourse and communion with the Holy Spirit, so that what lies in the heart of God, these things that the natural man knows nothing about, the things which God has prepared for them that love Him, might be the present and precious portion of people like you and me—committed people, according to Malachi, and prayerful people according to 1 Kings 18. I am persuaded of this, dear brethren, that the way into these things is by prayer, committal, and communion, the communion of the Holy Spirit.

Well, God says, “Prove me now”. Who is He addressing? I would say to each individual. He is addressing you. I would say to myself that He is addressing me, that we may prove Him together, and that, as His blessing pours in, there may be a commensurate answer in the Spirit’s power in praise and response and fervent love for Himself. May
God help us in this, for Christ’s sake.

This scripture in Acts has often been read, and no doubt many here will recall ministry as to it, which would not be out of our minds as we come together because the ministry that the Lord gives does not ‘date’. We are in this dispensation, this present time, which was inaugurated long ago by the coming of the Spirit, and the ministry that Paul gave at Corinth, Thessalonica, and elsewhere is still living and has current application, in spite of the breakdown. Down the centuries spiritual men have clung to the Scriptures and so should we, dear brethren, cling to the Scriptures. Then the ministry that the Lord gave through Mr. Darby, Mr. Raven, Mr. Taylor, and others we are to cling to. Brethren recall such ministry in their minds in an occasion like this and the occasion is thus enriched.

You may say that is rather mysterious. One may speak, but a good deal is passing through the brethren’s minds as the Scripture is read, and it provides a vein for the Spirit to work at. Therefore we all contribute to the occasion, dear brethren. We are here together, physically together, and normally in our minds and thinking we are together, and thus the occasion becomes augmented.

One may speak, but that in itself is a relatively small matter, what is important is the weight of substance, one might say the weight of gold, that is present in the occasion. The Spirit can take it—such is His power, such is the mystery, the inscrutability, of His ways—He can take what is in your heart and mine and cause it to be actually expressed, to be formulated into words. Have you not known it in the reading of the Scriptures, in a meeting of this kind? This I think would be a normal activity of the Spirit.

I have read this section as to Peter and John and one thing that has been said about the section is that in it there is something of a delineation of the dispensation. In Peter and what he represents, and in John and what he represents, there is something of a pattern of the dispensation, involving both kingdom and family thoughts. I would like to speak perhaps a little differently, that is, not exactly to follow the same ground. I trust it will not be incompatible with what has been said before, in fact maybe it has been said before. I am thinking of Peter as representing energy, and John as representing what is reflective; and I think it is right, dear brethren, to say that these two features are to mark the end of the dispensation. Indeed it has been intended that they should be present throughout the dispensation. In the divine call, in the Lord’s calling of the apostles, He was selective. Although it may have appeared differently, He selected carefully. In one gospel, you remember, He prayed through the night before. He selected Peter and He selected John— Peter, as I say, represents something of energy, living energy. He did not have to be prodded on the day of Pentecost to get up and speak. On that momentous day the twelve did not go into committee to decide to nominate one of their number to speak—Peter in the energy of
the Spirit got up and he spoke.

That is not to be unknown by us, dear brethren. The occasion comes round for the ministry meeting; energy is not to be an unknown element there; it is to be present. Peter was marked by that. Whilst we know that he was marked by it naturally, perhaps a certain impetuosity too, he was also, I think, marked by it spiritually; God made him that way. What he was, God used, and here Peter takes the lead. He was the first to speak here; Peter and John go up and Peter is the one who speaks, representing preparedness to go into things, to set something on. Often in the meeting for ministry one waits for a ‘warming-up word’, if one could use that expression, for someone to start. I think the Lord would help us all to start. It may be simple; perhaps your impression is not very much you might once have asked what were five loaves and two small fishes with all those thousands of brethren. Do you think that, with that little bit, you would have decided to speak in the ministry meeting that day, or do you think you would have said, ‘Let someone else speak; let him start and I will see if my word fits in’?. These things are not unknown to us, dear brethren; we are all the same, though some are ahead of us—thank God for them! To some the experience is deeper and more real, therefore when they speak there is a certain weight, and a kind of inner ability to touch the affections of the saints, that others of us do not have. But in the measure in which we are real we shall touch what is real; “deep calleth unto deep” (Psalm 42: 7); that scripture may have many applications, but it does involve that something that is said from the depths of the heart would affect the depths of the heart in another. On the other hand, if I am superficial, if my part, so to speak, has little depth and feeling (God forbid it should be so!), it is likely to
affect others only superficially.

So Peter represents energy. As I have said, it probably marked him naturally even before the Lord called him. But Peter developed spiritual energy too and this is seen at the beginning of the Acts. It is also seen at the end of his life as he wrote his second epistle; twice there he speaks of stirring up the saints (2 Peter 1: 13; 3: 1). Peter represents the kind of person that stirs you as he speaks. The preaching may have that character. It is good, dear brethren; it should not die amongst us; energy in the service should not die. But let it be real, I mean energy by the Spirit. Peter is prepared to speak, and that element is to go on with us. Especially when we are small and feel weak, we are to maintain an inner fire, if one might so say. How do you maintain that? We sometimes sing—
‘Lord, kindle within us a holy desire,
Like that which was found in Thy people of old.

Who tasted Thy love, and whose hearts were an fire’. Can you not taste His love? Can you not, in your soul, spend a few minutes before the meeting drinking in afresh something of the love of Christ? When you get to the meeting you will not wait five minutes for a hymn, you will have something, you will go with a certain fire, something already ignited. It is intended to be so with us, dear brethren, in brothers and sisters. It should not be lacking; like the wood offering, it should be brought. Keep the fire burning; bring it, so that things go through with a living character. We may feel sometimes that it is not so, but then we are intended to be stimulated; the Lord would strengthen and stimulate us. You see, someone has got to set things on, someone has to carry things, someone has to speak. I confess to my shame that I once sat through a whole ministry meeting and none of us gave

a word, and what I came to afterwards, and I just mention it simply, was that anything that had magnified Christ would have been worth while that night, “For the spirit of prophecy is the testimony of Jesus”, Revelation 19: 10. Could no one say something about the glory of Christ? Was I in a rebellious spirit? We are to come together to edify one another, and it does involve a certain energy, spiritually drawn on, and my impression is that John provides the reservoir from whence it is drawn.

So I do not want to speak about Peter and John exactly as two separate persons, but as representing two ideas which are to be present in each of us. There is the reflective John. Possibly, you could sit with him and he might hardly say a word to you; he would reflect, he seems to be of that character. “We have contemplated his glory, a glory as of an only-begotten with a father, full of grace and truth” (John 1: 14); that is John. That is not to be missing from us either, in fact it is John who supports Peter, John is behind Peter. There is to be with us a chewing of the cud, a moving of the jaws, and things going on inside one. That is the reflective side; things are formed, enter into the constitution, and provide the energy that becomes evident in a person. These two elements, dear brethren, are to develop with us. Do not neglect John; do not neglect this reflective side. When you read the ministry, when you read a monthly book, see if you can put it down and think about it before you go and get the coffee, or whatever has to be done next. Think about it, get the gain of it, give it time to enter into your constitution, let it find a lodging place.
It may work slowly; those cows in the field, you see them sitting there and chewing the cud, over it goes, round it goes, over and over, and it

is assimilated. That word you read, that word you heard, that preaching, learn to ponder it, recall it and think about it again. That is what John did, I think, in principle. There may be some difference between reflection and contemplation, because in the latter you are looking at some one, but with both the idea is there of what takes time, what can go on quietly and in secret, when things are being formed in you and when the constitution is being built up. In due time it will emerge in energy, and the spoken word will exhibit some evidence of life, some evidence of vigour.

These things, dear brethren, go through the whole dispensation, and they are to go through in you and in me, otherwise in some part of us we shall lack, we shall be at a loss, we shall, so to speak, run out of steam. There have been locomotives in the old days of the railways which ran out of steam. Some of the early locomotive engineers built engines with big cylinders thinking they would get more power, but the boiler was not big enough when the locomotive worked hard, to supply the cylinders with steam—when such an engine came to a gradient with a heavy load on, it steadily ground to a halt. The engine was all right but the steam was not there, and a famous engineer (if I might digress, you will pardon me) re-thought the whole idea by building a locomotive with a big boiler and relatively small cylinders. O, you might say, it has not got much power with those small cylinders, but it could steam, it could keep going when the others stopped; it kept going, it had a substantial source of energy in the fire and in the boiler. It was a success, and that class of locomotive lasted for years. That is the intention, that you should have a capacity, a reservoir, so that as we come together there is something that can come out. In divine things there should be with the believer a capacity, a reserve, that will back up and maintain things so that meetings and gatherings go through in power.

Well, perhaps our experience is variable, but the Lord would encourage us. This man in Acts 3 came into the gain of these things, and as coming into fellowship we are to come into the gain of these elements being present—and finally the man provided these elements in himself—he held Peter and John, he clung to these things. They represent, I say again, something of a delineation of the whole dispensation that is to go through. Will we run out of resources at the end, dear brethren? Will the word of God keep coming to us freshly? Will we be maintained by it? It is good to read the ministry, and the old ministries, and the Scriptures, the great framework on which everything hangs, and to keep within its bounds. But let the Spirit so work in you that it comes out, as it were, with the Spirit’s living impress on it. You may say, I am a sister and I do not speak. Yes, but it will show through you; it will show through your attitude, the way you follow the meeting, whether you are fresh. You may be a sister, but you may be adding to this occasion. What is going through your mind may be significantly adding to what is being said. Even if Paul was here and was speaking he would have regard for what was in you and the body of the saints. How true that is! How bound up together we are, dear brethren, what a mutual thing this is!

In a certain sense this scripture represents mutuality, too, a certain sovereignty in Peter and a preparedness to be second in John. These are elements which are not to be unknown to us, but the main thing I felt led to draw attention to was these two sides, energy by the maintenance of this reflective, ruminating kind of character. Learn

to think about things, try in between everything else to get some time for reflection. You will find that your constitution will be better for it, the meeting will be enriched, the saints will be enriched. When you meet someone you will have some water with you to wash the saints’ feet. How often one feels at a loss, ‘How are you today? How is your cold?’. And that is about all you can say, whereas coming together and seeing the saints it is intended that we should be able to touch one another in a spiritual sense.

Well, may the Lord help us in these things, dear brethren. As we take them on, as we get the gain of them, we shall be like this man of whom it says he ‘leaped’, and that is just why I read in Leviticus, because a leaper is to be appropriated. It says of the winged, crawling insects that if they had legs above their feet and could leap, then you could appropriate them. They are fine! That is material for the assembly—persons who can leave the earth; only for a little while perhaps; how difficult it is, is it not, dear brethren, to sustain a spiritual conversation for long? But if you can leave the earth for a little while, then you can be appropriated; the brethren can feed on you; you are really a person that soon will leave the earth, not for a little while, but for ever. You will not do that by leaping, of course; you will be taken, but there will have already been some moral experience of it. You say, Well, we left the earth for a little while. We got abstracted, we got caught up in that enquiry, in that reading, we got caught up just for a little while, and then something brought us back. Yes, but still we did leave it for a little while. You see the idea. This man became a leaper; he held to these two things. How glad the brethren would be to see him leap up to give a word. You can expect a good word

from him, it will contain the knowledge that cometh of reflection (Proverbs 8: 12). So it is intended that we should all contribute, and the evidence of reflection is seen in this side of energy that is continually needed. May the Lord bless these simple thoughts to us, dear brethren, for His name’s sake.

We should be encouraged to see what is open to us. Heaven was opened to Stephen. Heaven was opened to John. Notice that the word is “opened” in each case, implying the active agency of Another, as though in answer to faith and the need that was there. So to us the “opened door” of Philadelphia (Revelation 3: 8) would involve the precious privilege of the Supper and access into all the great thoughts of God. Not only is the door opened but we are welcome, as was said to John—“Come up here”, Revelation 4: 1. What privileges are open to us at the present time! The disciples were with the Lord on the mount of transfiguration and in Gethsemane we can be with Him in anticipation of the coming day of glory. If we suffer with Him, we shall also reign with Him. Suffering with Christ in view of the glory is open to us now and we can have access by faith and in the Spirit’s power into the light of that scene of glory above.
Kingston, Ont.
Oh bring them in, the supper feast is spread
And free to all!
God’s wondrous grace the lordly table laid
For great and small.
Come! is the invitation freely given
By Him who came from glory there in heaven.
The royal invitation comes to you;
Accept it now!
Extended by the Holy Spirit too
While grace allows.
No other feast with such provision made,
For with great cost has been the table laid.
Oh bring them in! The city yields its store
Of ruined man,
The crippled and the lame, the blind and poor,
From street and lane.
Three thousand brought by one great act of power
Into God’s house, while reigns the supper hour.
The hour of supper! What a word is this
To hungry souls.
More wondrous still, the fulness of God’s grace
Provides the whole!
Alone the cost was borne by His blest Son;
Alone by Him the wondrous work was done.
And while they crowded in on that great day
At Pentecost,
There still was room for others far away
In darkness lost.
The ways and fences of the nations still
Are searched, the house with many souls to fill.
Compel them in! Both power and love combine
The house to fill.
Oh hasten, yield the claims of Him divine
Awaiting still.
For ‘tis no common servant waits your choice,
‘Tis the blest Spirit—heed His heavenly voice.
The Servant had returned before to say
There still was room,
But goes once more into the distant way
To bring them in.
Nor yet has He returned—thy chance remains,
But only holds so long as He detains.
But yet, who knows the time when this will cease?
The offer done!
The last seat taken at the royal feast,
No empty one.
And you declined the invitation given;
Outside you must remain the bliss of heaven.
The hour of supper! Wondrous words of grace
Of Jesus still,
Speaking of blessing for the human race,
At God’s blest will,
Redemption wrought, forgiveness offered free,
Repent! believe the gospel sent to thee.
‘TOO SATISFIED’ An owner of cattle was going round inspecting his stock. We came to one herd and at his call they ambled in a slow procession out of one field to pasture in another. As we
walked on to see another herd he remarked, ‘I doubt whether they will come when I call; they are too satisfied with their pasture’.

Are you and I, as believers, ‘satisfied with our pasture’? One of the things that should keep the believer clear of the world, and the seductive call of the god of it, is that it is not good enough for him. Could you persuade Mephibosheth to give up David’s company, and David’s bountiful table, once more to return to Lodebar (‘no pasture’)? Would the recovered younger son of Luke 15 ever again forsake the father’s affections, and the rich provision of the father’s house, for the far country? Let us give ourselves, by the Spirit, to the full enjoyment of our inheritance, so that the call of the world finds no answer in our hearts—we are too satisfied with our pasture. There is another side—the truth of the cross (Galatians 6: 14) is also to keep us from the world. May the world that crucified our Lord always be a crucified place to us, and may we be crucified to it.

God has placed authority in the parents where it is most likely to be sympathetic, in the one who loves you most, and the disregard of that is, in principle, apostasy. “Without natural affection” (Romans 1: 31) is one mark of apostasy in the last days. I warn you, if you are a child, that if you disregard the authority and the claims of parents, you disregard the claims of Christ. I warn you to regard authority and recognise divinely ordered relationships.
